title: Order
hook: an ordered space helps an ordered mind

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: hakarat hatov, recognizing the good, like Ben Zoma's good guest. Your line was recognize the good. Whom did you name, out loud? Today, a word every Passover table already knows. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

Keys. Where are the keys? They were on the counter. They're not on the counter. Now the coat pockets, the couch cushions, yesterday's jeans, and somewhere in the middle of the hunt a morning can go from fine to furious. Ten minutes later they turn up in the fridge. Nothing about the morning was hard. It was just scattered, and the scatter got inside. Jewish teachers of character noticed that the drawer and the mind talk to each other. They put a trait on the list for it, and it shares its name with a dinner held every spring.
screen: `WHERE ARE THE KEYS?` → `FINE TO FURIOUS.` → `THE DRAWER AND THE MIND TALK.`

segments.voice: Seder. Order. It shows up in four places. First, the dinner. The Passover seder is called seder because it runs in an order: the steps of the evening have names, and some families chant the list of them at the start. The night that remembers leaving slavery is held together by a sequence. Freedom, at that table, is not chaos. It has steps. Second, the prayer book. The everyday Jewish prayer book is called a siddur, from the same root: an arranged thing, words set in order. And the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, is divided into sections called sedarim, orders. So the word runs through the table, the prayer book and the study hall. Third, the first chapter of Genesis. Read it for its verbs and you find a lot of separating and placing. God divides the light from the darkness, the waters above from the waters below, gathers the seas into one place so dry land appears. Then the plants each after its kind, and the lights set in the sky. Before any creature moves, everything has a place. Fourth, the trait. Mussar puts seder on the list of middot because outer order and inner order lean on each other. When your things have a place, your attention isn't spent hunting for them, and it's free for the people in front of you. Which brings back the word from earlier this week: middot are measures. Too little order and life spills everywhere. Too much and you're straightening the napkins while your guest is talking. The right measure is enough order to be free.
screen: `THE SEDER RUNS IN STEPS.` · `SIDDUR, SEDARIM: THE SAME ROOT.` · `IN GENESIS, EVERYTHING GETS A PLACE.` · `ENOUGH ORDER TO BE FREE.` · then, large: `ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tidy one drawer. If one is nearby, open it now. If not, picture one: the junk drawer, the bag you carry, the top of your desk. Take everything out, or picture taking it out. Look at each thing once. Does it belong here? Does it belong anywhere? Put back only what has a reason, each in a place you could find with your eyes closed. Go slowly. This is not a race, and the drawer doesn't need to be perfect. Notice what happens in your chest as the space clears. If you pray, you can bring the quiet of the sorting to God in your own words. If you don't, simply let your hands set things in place. The bell holds the time.
Seder. Order: the name of the Passover meal, the root of the siddur, and a Mussar trait, enough order to be free. Today's word.
Your line: order. Today, give one thing you're always hunting for, keys, glasses, a charger, a single home, and put it back there every time. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: In Mussar practice, Jews working on seder start with small, physical order, a drawer, a desk, a schedule, as a way to steady attention; the Passover seder itself follows named steps in a set order.

notes: Lexical claims: seder (order), siddur (arranged prayer book) and sedarim (orders of the Mishnah) share a root; confirm.
'Some families chant the list of the steps at the start'; confirm.
The Mishnah is described as 'the great early collection of Jewish law' without a date or a count of orders; confirm wording.
Order (seder) as a trait on Mendel of Satanov's list; confirm.
